r.정치 구도: Uzbekistan is a presidential system with power heavily concentrated in the president. For 25 years after independence in 1991, one leader kept the country largely closed off; after a change of leadership in 2016 came an opening that included freeing the currency, easing visas and settling border disputes with neighbors. Parliament still has no party that genuinely opposes the government, and the media and civil society remain tightly controlled. A new constitution approved by referendum in 2023 lengthened the presidential term from five years to seven and reset the incumbent's term count, and a snap election followed straight away. In 2022, protests in the western autonomous republic of Karakalpakstan against a draft amendment that would have curbed its autonomy were put down with deadly force, and the government ultimately dropped those provisions.

t.why: It sits at the heart of Central Asia and borders all of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Afghanistan. As the region's most populous country, it is central to talks with its neighbors over water, borders and transport routes. It must share the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers with upstream states, and Soviet-era irrigation of cotton fields drained much of the Aral Sea. Lacking a route to the sea, it is investing in the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, on which construction began in December 2024, and in plans for a line through Afghanistan to Pakistani ports. It left the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organization in 2012 and has joined the Eurasian Economic Union only as an observer since 2020, balancing between Russia, China and the West.
t.rel: A double-landlocked country in the heart of Central Asia: reaching the sea means crossing two borders. Since 2016 it has greatly improved relations with its neighbors by settling border and water issues.
t.korea: The two countries established diplomatic relations in 1992 and upgraded ties to a 'special strategic partnership' in 2019. Because the Soviet Union forcibly deported ethnic Koreans from the Russian Far East to Central Asia in 1937, more than 170,000 Koryo-saram still live in Uzbekistan, the largest such community in any country. The car plant Daewoo built in Asaka in the east in the 1990s is the root of what is now the country's biggest automaker. Lotte Chemical and KOGAS teamed up with Uzbekistan's state oil and gas company to build a gas chemical complex at the Surgil field in the west, which began operating in 2016. Many Uzbeks work in South Korea under its Employment Permit System, and critical-mineral supply chains have recently become a new focus of cooperation.
t.know: Uzbekistan is one of only two double-landlocked countries in the world.
etext: Navoi Mining and Metallurgical Company is one of the world's top gold producers, and Almalyk MMC is expanding a large copper mine. When gold prices rise, gold props up both exports and the state budget.

Letting the market set the exchange rate and freeing foreign-currency transactions in 2017 brought a rapid rise in foreign investment and trade. Sales of state companies, tax reform and talks to join the World Trade Organization (WTO) are continuing.

For years the state forced citizens to pick cotton, drawing an international boycott. After the ILO found systemic forced labor had ended in the 2021 harvest, the boycott was lifted in 2022, and the country now aims to sell yarn and clothing rather than raw cotton.

Distance from the sea makes logistics expensive, and a shortage of jobs leaves many families relying on money sent home by relatives working in Russia and elsewhere. State companies still loom large, and water scarcity leaves farming vulnerable to climate change.
